explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. John 13:22 says, "The disciples looked at one another, perplexed as to which of them He meant." They didn't know which of them He meant. I think that was a very quiet, awkward dinner table.

That's right, friend. "The disciples looked at one another, perplexed as to which of them He meant." They had no idea. I think every one of them was checking every other face and hoping their own looked innocent.

explanations.answer: Ask Jesus which one He means
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Peter motioned to the disciple at Jesus' side to ask Jesus which one He was talking about. I think that's like a man trying to get a waiter's attention in a packed restaurant. Then the disciple leaned back and asked.

explanations.answer: Get up and guard the door
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a door, friend. John 13:24 says Peter motioned to the disciple to ask Jesus which one He was talking about. That's a question, not a guard post.

Close, but Peter wanted a question asked, not a hush. The text says he motioned to the disciple "…to ask Jesus which one He was talking about." That's a nudge toward talking. A man waving his hands around is not a man saying "stay calm."

explanations.answer: He'll give that one a dipped morsel
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Jesus answered, "It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it." Then He dipped the morsel and gave it away. The answer was a sign and not a name, and it was given right there at the table.

explanations.answer: He'll point to that one at the table
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text doesn't say Jesus pointed. He gave the sign: "It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it." Then He dipped it and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot.

explanations.answer: He'll call that one by name
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. In answer to the question, Jesus said, "It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it." He gave a sign instead of saying a name out loud. Then He gave the morsel to Judas.
Yes, baker! Jesus gave the dipped morsel to Judas son of Simon Iscariot. Judas is the disciple who kept the money bag (John 13:29). Right after he took it, Jesus spoke to him.

Thomas doesn't show up anywhere in this passage, friend. The text says Jesus dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot. It's an easy name to grab when you're guessing, but it isn't the one John gives.
Andrew isn't named in this passage, friend. John 13:26 says Jesus gave the morsel to "…Judas son of Simon Iscariot." That's the name that goes in the blank. Nice try, though.

You got it, baker. John 13:28 says, "But no one at the table knew why Jesus had said this to him." Not one person at the table knew why. I think they were all just as lost as I am when somebody says "it's a quick fix" and hands me a wrench.

Not this time, friend. The text says, "But no one at the table knew why Jesus had said this to him." So nobody had it figured out. The disciples were guessing, and the next verse shows what they guessed.

explanations.answer: Buy what's needed for the feast
explanations.explanation: Right, baker! Because Judas kept the money bag, some thought Jesus was telling him "…to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor." Makes sense for a guy holding the cash. When I hear "go quickly," I figure it's a cookie run.

explanations.answer: Pay the owner of the house
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention paying the owner of the house, friend. John 13:29 says some thought Jesus was telling Judas "…to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor." Paying an owner isn't one of those guesses.

The text doesn't say anything about hiding the bag, friend. Some thought Jesus was telling Judas "…to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor." Since Judas kept the money bag, the guesses it gives are about buying and giving, not hiding.

explanations.answer: He goes out into the night
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. "As soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out into the night." The text says as soon as. This is one of the heavier lines in the passage, and I think it's okay to let it sit for a second.

explanations.answer: He hands Jesus the money bag
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. Judas kept the money bag, but the verse says, "As soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out into the night." Nothing about a bag changing hands. Judas just left.

explanations.answer: He sits back down and stays quiet
explanations.explanation: No, Judas didn't stay, friend. John 13:30 says, "As soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out into the night." He went out. Going out into the night is the opposite of sitting back down.
Not quite, friend. Jesus says God "…will also glorify the Son in Himself—and will glorify Him at once." At once is the opposite of a long wait. So the answer here is no.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, "…and will glorify Him at once." There's no long wait in His words. At once means right away, like when the timer goes off and you're already at the oven door.
Yes, baker! Jesus says, "Where I am going, you cannot come." He had said the same thing to the Jews earlier. The disciples would look for Him, and this is what He tells them about where He's headed.
That isn't in the text, friend. What Jesus says is, "Where I am going, you cannot come." He doesn't mention sending for anybody. Those are a heavy few words to hear at supper.

explanations.answer: It's only a short walk away
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. Jesus says, "Where I am going, you cannot come." That's the whole line, and I think it doesn't sound like a stroll around the block.

That's right, baker! Jesus says, "A new commandment I give you: Love one another." It's a short sentence, but it's the one He chose to give them right here at the table. I could stamp it on a whole batch.
Good word, friend, but it's not the one here. The verse says, "A new commandment I give you: Love one another." So love goes in the blank. That's the command Jesus gave the disciples in that room.
Teaching is a fine thing, friend, but Jesus didn't say it here. John 13:34 says, "A new commandment I give you: Love one another." Love is the word He used.

explanations.answer: The way He has loved them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Jesus says, "As I have loved you, so you also must love one another." He doesn't just give them the command. He points to how He has loved them as the example. That's a pretty high bar, and it's the one He set.
These verses don't mention the prophets, friend. Jesus says, "As I have loved you, so you also must love one another." The example He holds up is His own love for them.

Moses, Israel's leader, isn't mentioned in this passage, friend. What Jesus says is, "As I have loved you, so you also must love one another." His own love for them is the example. That's what He points to.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another." Love is the thing that shows. I'd keep it simple too, since it's the one thing everybody can see.
Not this time, friend. Jesus says, "By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another." So the statement is true. Love for one another is how everyone will know.

Yes, baker! Simon Peter, one of the disciples, asks, "Lord, where are You going?" Jesus had just said they could not come where He was going. So Peter asks the question that was probably on everybody's mind. I think I'd have asked the same thing, only louder.

explanations.answer: Lord when will You come back
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in the text, friend. Peter asks, "Lord, where are You going?" His question is about the place, not about a return. I think he wanted to know where Jesus was headed.

explanations.answer: Lord who will lead us now
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't record Peter asking that, friend. John 13:36 says Simon Peter asked, "Lord, where are You going?" It's a question about where Jesus is going.
Not quite, friend. Jesus says Peter cannot follow Him now but will follow later, and Peter keeps going. He asks, "Lord, why can't I follow You now?" That's not a man who drops it.
That's right, baker. Peter says, "Lord, why can't I follow You now?" He asks something more. I'd have asked a lot of questions too, probably with my mustache flapping.

explanations.answer: To lay down his life for Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Peter says, "I will lay down my life for You." That's a huge promise to make. Jesus answers it with a question, and the next lines show where it goes.
That's not in the text, friend. What Peter promises is, "I will lay down my life for You." It's a promise about himself and nothing else. The words are about his own life.

explanations.answer: To bring Judas back to Him
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't say anything like that, friend. His promise is, "I will lay down my life for You." Judas had already gone out into the night (John 13:30). Peter's words are about his own life.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "…before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." I think this one stings, and I'm not going to joke about it. Peter had just promised everything, and Jesus told him what was coming.
Praise would be a lot nicer, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says. He tells Peter, "…before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." I think this is a heavy moment, so let's take it gently.

Defend sounds like something Peter would want, friend, but that's not the word. Jesus says, "…before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." I think that's a hard thing to hear from Him, right after Peter said he would lay down his life.
